title: Displacement of families from Pakistan-occupied areas
place_name: Mirpur, Muzaffarabad, Bhimber, Kotli and other occupied areas
summary: The 1947 war displaced 31,619 families from areas that came under Pakistani occupation, according to the Union government. Of these, 26,319 families registered and settled in Jammu and Kashmir, and 5,300 moved to other parts of India. Many still await full rehabilitation.

title: Invasion of Muzaffarabad and killings at Domel
summary: On 22 October 1947 tribal lashkars, armed, transported and led by Pakistan Army officers, crossed into Jammu and Kashmir and took Muzaffarabad within days. Hindu and Sikh residents and refugees were killed, their homes looted and burnt, and many women abducted. Men rounded up near Domel were shot and their bodies thrown into the river. India marks 22 October as a Black Day for the invasion.

title: Sack of Baramulla
place_name: Baramulla, including St Joseph's Convent and hospital
victim_community: Hindu, Sikh, Christian and Muslim residents
summary: The lashkars reached Baramulla on 26 October 1947 and spent days looting the town instead of pressing on to Srinagar. Raiders stormed St Joseph's Convent and its hospital, killing nuns, staff and patients. Survivors estimated that about 3,000 townspeople were killed. The delay gave India time to fly troops into Srinagar.

title: Indian troops airlifted to Srinagar after accession
summary: Maharaja Hari Singh signed the Instrument of Accession to India on 26 October 1947. From the morning of 27 October the Indian Army flew its first troops into Srinagar airfield to stop the advance of the invaders on the city. The airlift is regarded as the step that saved Srinagar.

title: Fall of Bhimber
summary: Bhimber fell to Pakistan-backed forces in the early hours of 28 October 1947, the first town in the south of the state to be captured. Accounts describe men being killed and women and children taken hostage. No reliable toll has been found.

title: Killings of prisoners at Alibeg camp
summary: Hindu and Sikh survivors from Mirpur and nearby areas were held in a gurdwara at Alibeg that Pakistani forces turned into a prison camp. Many were killed and others died of disease and hunger. The Red Cross reached the camp in early 1948 and about 1,600 survivors were moved to India in March 1948.

title: Gilgit Scouts revolt and seizure of Gilgit
summary: On 1 November 1947 the Gilgit Scouts revolted, arrested the state's Governor and declared for Pakistan, which took over the area soon after. The revolt cut Gilgit off from the state and opened the way for attacks on Skardu and Ladakh.

title: Rajouri massacre
summary: Pakistani troops and raiders captured Rajouri on 7 November 1947, when the town was crowded with Hindu and Sikh refugees from the west. Killings peaked around Diwali on 11 and 12 November, and many women took their own lives to avoid capture. The town remained under occupation until the Indian Army retook it on 12 to 13 April 1948.

title: Battle of Shalateng
summary: Indian troops routed the main body of the invaders at Shalateng on the edge of Srinagar on 7 November 1947. The victory ended the threat to the city and opened the way to retake Baramulla and Uri.

title: Siege of Poonch
summary: Poonch, crowded with refugees, was surrounded by Pakistani forces from late November 1947. Under Brigadier Pritam Singh the garrison and residents built an airstrip in about a week, and supplies came in by air from December 1947 despite shelling. The siege was broken in November 1948 when a relief force linked up with the garrison.

title: Mirpur massacre
summary: Mirpur, home to some 25,000 to 30,000 Hindus and Sikhs including refugees, fell to Pakistani forces and raiders on 25 November 1947 after a night of shelling. Thousands were killed within a day and many women took their own lives. About 3,500 survivors were held at a camp at Alibeg, while others reached Jammu on foot.

title: Battle of Naushera
summary: In February 1948 the 50 Parachute Brigade under Brigadier Mohammad Usman beat back a major Pakistani assault on Naushera. The brigade later retook Jhangar.

title: Indian Army retakes Rajouri
summary: Indian troops recaptured Rajouri on 12 to 13 April 1948 after five months of occupation. They found the town ruined and its Hindu and Sikh population largely killed or gone.

title: Brigadier Mohammad Usman killed at Jhangar
summary: Brigadier Mohammad Usman, who had held Naushera and retaken Jhangar, was killed by a Pakistani shell on 3 July 1948. He remains the highest-ranking Indian officer killed in battle, and the Army marks Jhangar Day in his memory.

title: Fall of Skardu and killing of the garrison
victim_community: Hindu and Sikh refugees and soldiers
summary: The 6th Jammu and Kashmir Infantry under Lt Col Sher Jung Thapa held Skardu fort for about six months against forces from Gilgit. Out of food and ammunition, the garrison surrendered on 14 August 1948. Soldiers and the refugees sheltering with them were then killed, and women in the garrison took their own lives. Thapa was taken prisoner.

title: Operation Bison, tanks at Zoji La
summary: On 1 November 1948 Indian light tanks crossed Zoji La at more than 11,500 feet and surprised the Pakistani-backed forces holding the pass. The attack reopened the road to Kargil and Ladakh.

title: Ceasefire ends the first war
summary: A UN-brokered ceasefire took effect at midnight on 1 January 1949. Pakistan was left in occupation of Mirpur, Muzaffarabad, parts of Poonch and the Gilgit region. The ceasefire line was fixed by the Karachi Agreement of July 1949.

title: Operation Gibraltar, Pakistani infiltration into Kashmir
place_name: Ceasefire line from Kargil to Mendhar
summary: From the night of 5 August 1965 Pakistan sent armed infiltrators, many of them soldiers dressed as locals, across the ceasefire line through routes in Gurez, Tithwal, Uri, Poonch, Rajouri and Kargil. The plan was to start an uprising in the Valley. Local people did not rise and often reported the infiltrators to the authorities, and the operation failed.

title: Indian paratroopers capture the Haji Pir pass
summary: To cut the main infiltration route into the Valley, 1 Para under Major Ranjit Singh Dyal climbed about 4,000 feet overnight and took the Haji Pir pass on the morning of 28 August 1965. Dyal received the Maha Vir Chakra. The pass was handed back to Pakistan under the Tashkent Declaration of 1966.

title: Operation Grand Slam, Pakistani armoured attack at Chhamb
summary: At 4 am on 1 September 1965 Pakistan attacked on the Chhamb and Akhnoor axis with an infantry division and Patton tanks, aiming to cut the road linking Jammu to the Valley. Chhamb fell on 2 September and Jaurian on 4 September. The advance was halted short of Akhnoor as India opened new fronts in Punjab.

title: Ceasefire ends the 1965 war
place_name: Jammu and Kashmir and the Punjab front
summary: A UN-backed ceasefire took effect on 23 September 1965. Under the Tashkent Declaration signed on 10 January 1966, both sides pulled back to positions held before 5 August 1965, which meant India returned the Haji Pir pass.

title: Hijacking of Indian Airlines flight Ganga to Lahore
place_name: Srinagar to Jammu flight, taken to Lahore
summary: On 30 January 1971 two members of the National Liberation Front, Hashim Qureshi and his cousin, hijacked the Indian Airlines Fokker Friendship Ganga soon after take-off from Srinagar and forced it to land at Lahore. Passengers and crew were sent back to India, but the aircraft was destroyed on the ground in Lahore. India responded by banning Pakistani flights over its territory, which hampered Pakistan later that year.

title: Turtuk and nearby villages retaken in Ladakh
place_name: Turtuk, Chalunkha, Thang and Takshi, Nubra
summary: In December 1971 troops led by Major Chewang Rinchen of the Ladakh Scouts advanced about 22 km through mountains in winter, without artillery support. They retook more than 800 sq km held by Pakistan since 1948, including the villages of Turtuk, Chalunkha, Thang and Takshi.

title: Battle of Chhamb, 1971
summary: On the night of 3 to 4 December 1971 Pakistan attacked in the Chhamb sector with a strong force, alongside air strikes on Indian airfields that opened the war in the west. India lost Chhamb for the second time in six years.

title: Simla Agreement and the Line of Control
summary: India and Pakistan signed the Simla Agreement on 2 July 1972 after the 1971 war. The ceasefire line at the end of the 1971 war became the Line of Control, and both sides agreed to settle differences bilaterally.

title: Abduction and killing of diplomat Ravindra Mhatre in Birmingham
summary: In February 1984 Indian diplomat Ravindra Mhatre was abducted in Birmingham by militants who demanded the release of JKLF founder Maqbool Bhat, and was then killed. Maqbool Bhat was hanged in Delhi soon after.

title: Operation Meghdoot secures the Siachen glacier
place_name: Bilafond La and Sia La, Saltoro Ridge
summary: On 13 April 1984, Baisakhi day, the Indian Army and Air Force began Operation Meghdoot and took the main passes of the Saltoro Ridge, Bilafond La and Sia La. The move pre-empted a Pakistani plan to occupy the heights, and India has held the Siachen glacier since.

title: Anantnag riots against Kashmiri Pandits
place_name: Wanpoh, Bijbehara, Akura and other villages of Anantnag
summary: From around 20 February 1986 mobs in Anantnag district attacked Kashmiri Pandit homes, shops and temples, starting at Wanpoh and spreading to Bijbehara and other villages. Temples were desecrated and burnt and houses looted. The riots are widely seen as an early warning of the 1990 exodus.

title: Operation Rajiv, capture of Quaid post on Siachen
summary: In June 1987 a party of 8 JAK LI attacked Quaid post, a Pakistani position overlooking Indian posts on Siachen, after two nights of artillery fire on 25 and 26 June. Naib Subedar Bana Singh led the final assault and received the Param Vir Chakra, and the post was renamed Bana Top.

title: Bomb blasts at Srinagar Telegraph Office and Golf Course
place_name: Central Telegraph Office and Golf Course, Srinagar
summary: On 31 July 1988 JKLF militants set off two bombs in Srinagar, one at the Central Telegraph Office and one at the Golf Course. The blasts are usually taken as the start of the armed insurgency in the Valley.

title: Killing of National Conference leader Mohammad Yusuf Halwai
summary: Mohammad Yusuf Halwai, a National Conference leader, was shot dead in daylight in downtown Srinagar on 21 August 1989. He is often described as the first political victim of the militancy in the Valley.

title: Killing of Tika Lal Taploo
summary: Tika Lal Taploo, a High Court advocate and vice-president of the BJP in the state, was shot dead in Srinagar on 14 September 1989. He was the first prominent Kashmiri Pandit leader to be killed, and his death spread fear through the community. The JKLF was blamed but the case stayed unsolved for decades.

title: Killing of retired judge Neelkanth Ganjoo
place_name: Hari Singh High Street, near the High Court, Srinagar
summary: Neelkanth Ganjoo, the judge who had sentenced JKLF founder Maqbool Bhat to death, was shot dead near the High Court in Srinagar on 4 November 1989. Suspicion fell on the JKLF but no one was arrested. The State Investigation Agency reopened the case in 2023.

title: Abduction of Rubaiya Sayeed and release of five militants
summary: Rubaiya Sayeed, daughter of Union Home Minister Mufti Mohammad Sayeed, was abducted in Srinagar on 8 December 1989. She was freed on 13 December after the government released five jailed JKLF militants. The exchange is widely seen as having emboldened armed groups. She later identified JKLF chief Yasin Malik in court as one of her abductors.

title: Killing of advocate Prem Nath Bhat
summary: Advocate Prem Nath Bhat was shot dead by militants at Khah Bazar in Anantnag on 27 December 1989. His killing came days before the mass flight of Kashmiri Pandits from the Valley in January 1990.
